text: An interactive learning tool for exploring how gravitational systems evolve over time

Educational model
Not a real collision forecast

Introduce the simulator as a learning-focused physics project. The visual shows a result from the team’s own simulation workflow. Set the boundary early: this is an illustrative model, not a prediction of a real galaxy collision.
Pairwise gravity becomes expensive as the number of particles grows
Direct gravity checks every particle pair at every simulation step.
More particles make a simple educational simulation slower and harder to explore.
Learners need visible outputs that connect numerical settings to motion over time.

Explain the core computational challenge. Each particle feels gravity from all others, so a direct calculation quickly becomes costly as particle counts increase. Students need a way to see the tradeoff between fidelity and computation without treating the result as astrophysical prediction.
Approximate distant groups of particles while keeping nearby interactions detailed
Set duration, timestep, total particle count, and starting separation.
Build an octree and use Barnes–Hut force approximations during the simulation.
Write positions to CSV, then render colored plots and an animation.
A simplified model for exploring numerical physics through a visible two-group interaction

The Barnes–Hut method groups distant particles into tree nodes. Instead of evaluating every distant particle individually, the simulator uses a summarized gravitational contribution. The user controls the run and studies the resulting snapshots.
Built for people learning physics, gravity, and computational simulation
Explore how initial conditions and timesteps change a simulation.
Use a compact example to connect code, numerical methods, and physical intuition.
Inspect a working C++ implementation and visualization pipeline.
Example: run 256 particles, export CSV snapshots, then follow the two colored groups through the rendered sequence.

Describe the use case in concrete terms. A student runs the supplied example with 256 particles, time one, timestep 0.01, and separation 10. The simulator saves positions; the plotting workflow turns those positions into a sequence the student can inspect.
Role of AI or machine learning
No AI or machine learning is used in the current simulator
Barnes–Hut approximation, numerical integration, and visualization scripts.
Simulation duration, timestep, particle count, separation, and model configuration.
Choose settings, run experiments, and interpret outputs in their educational context.

Be direct: the current project is a physics simulation, not an AI product. The user supplies parameters, the program computes a model, and the user interprets the output. This makes the project’s technical contribution clear and avoids overstating capabilities.
A C++20 command-line workflow from inputs to an inspectable visual result
Tech stack: C++20, Apple Clang, CSV, plotting scripts, and FFmpeg video output

Walk judges through the workflow left to right. The tree groups particles spatially, Barnes–Hut approximates distant forces, and the integrator advances motion. Snapshots are written to CSV before the separate plotting and video steps.
Planned research support, not an implemented project feature
The simulator runs entirely from configured inputs. No TinyFish connection is built or verified.
Gather selected public astronomy examples or properties to provide scenario context and setting suggestions.

State the distinction clearly. TinyFish is not part of the current build. A future version could use it to gather publicly available astronomy material from selected sources, helping users choose scenarios and understand the context behind simulation inputs.
A clearer bridge from simulation settings to visible motion
Students can connect parameters with changing positions across a run.
Educators gain a compact example of approximation in computational physics.
CSV snapshots, rendered frames, a showcase image, and a video are present in the project workspace.
No outcome statistics are claimed. These benefits are expected educational value, not measured impact.

Frame benefits as likely learning value rather than measured outcomes. Report the available evidence precisely: project materials contain saved CSV snapshots, an image, and an approximately ten-second showcase video. No user-study metrics or independent performance benchmarks are claimed.
The core simulation and visualization workflow already run locally
CLI simulator, parameter options, CSV snapshots, plotting frames, image, and MP4 workflow.
Apple Clang, CMake, Python with NumPy and Matplotlib, plus FFmpeg for video output.
Finish README review and package a guided example run for students and educators.

Focus on what exists. The project has a C++20 CLI, named options, even-particle validation, CSV output, and visualization scripts. A practical next step is to polish documentation and add a reproducible command sequence or simple parameter presets.
Practical improvements beyond the hackathon prototype
Add curated parameter presets and short questions that prompt observation.
Show Barnes–Hut and direct-summation behavior side by side on small cases.
Propose TinyFish-supported source gathering for selected public astronomy context.

These are future ideas, not current features. Keep them tied to the project’s educational purpose: easier parameter exploration, clearer comparison of approximate and direct methods, and optional sourced context through a future TinyFish workflow.
